sites.name: Fort Hill
sites.summary: A wall of earth and stone running more than a mile and a half around the rim of a steep, flat-topped hill, enclosing 48 acres. Squier and Davis surveyed it in 1846. It stands in old forest today, which is why aerial photographs show nothing and LiDAR shows all of it.
notes: The wall follows the rim of the hill all the way around; in the relief it shows as a bright line just inside the edge of the plateau, with the plate's gateways as gaps.
Forest hides it from aerial photographs. Switch the ground to 'Aerial photograph' to compare.

Placed from four hand-picked points (the two tips and two corners), then fitted to the wall: it stands about 0.2 m above the ground 12 m to either side after a tight relief filter, against −0.09 m for random placements.

plate.source: Squier & Davis 1848, Plate V (surveyed by E. G. Squier and E. H. Davis, 1846). Scan: Internet Archive ancientmonuments00squi leaf n68.
plate.label: Plate V

sites.name: Fudge Site
sites.summary: A 31-acre earthwork rectangle that James McBride surveyed in 1847. The walls have been plowed down, and the 9 ft central mound was dug out in the late 1920s.
notes: The relief shows two parallel raised bands 320 m apart. The north one stands about 0.45 m above the ground 25 m to either side, the south one about 0.3 m. The plate puts the walls 1080 ft (329 m) apart.
Fitting the plate's walls to the relief gives 0.47 m per plate pixel, within 2% of the plate's own labeled sizes.
A county road now crosses the north third of the enclosure. A quarry lake sits where the southern half of the east wall should be.
NRHP 07000213, listed 2007 (Fudge Site).

plate.source: Squier & Davis 1848, Plate XXXIII No. 2 (surveyed by James McBride, 1847). Scan: Internet Archive ancientmonuments00squi leaf n203.
plate.label: Plate XXXIII No. 2

sites.name: High Bank Works
sites.summary: A 20-acre circle joined to an 18-acre octagon, with smaller circles and a long avenue of parallel walls running south. Squier and Davis surveyed it in 1846. It is the only other Hopewell circle-and-octagon besides Newark, and is part of Hopewell Culture National Historical Park.
notes: The great circle and the octagon both show as faint low rises in the relief. The fitted plate puts the circle at about 162 m radius, close to the plate's 20 acres.
The plate is drawn close to true north: the fit turns it under 2 degrees.
The plate's 'natural bank' along the terrace edge sits roughly 90 m west of the edge in the LiDAR. The walls, not the bank, set the fit.
A rail embankment runs just northeast of the octagon. Not yet checked here: the small circles and the long avenue to the south.

plate.source: Squier & Davis 1848, Plate XVI (surveyed by E. G. Squier and E. H. Davis, 1846). Scan: Internet Archive ancientmonuments00squi leaf n126.
plate.label: Plate XVI

sites.name: Hopeton Works
sites.summary: A 20-acre circle joined to a 20-acre square, with parallel walls running 2400 ft toward the Scioto. Squier and Davis surveyed it in 1846. It is now part of Hopewell Culture National Historical Park.
notes: The circle and the square both show as low rises in the relief. The circle is about 300 m across, close to the plate's 1050 ft (320 m).
The plate draws the square about 15% smaller than its own 900 ft label. The overlay is rubber-sheeted so that the circle and the square each sit on their LiDAR walls.
The plate is rotated about 34 degrees from page-up to true north.

plate.source: Squier & Davis 1848, Plate XVII (surveyed by E. G. Squier and E. H. Davis, 1846). Scan: Internet Archive ancientmonuments00squi leaf n129.
plate.label: Plate XVII

sites.name: Marietta Works
sites.summary: Two walled squares of 50 and 27 acres, flat-topped mounds and a graded way down to the Muskingum, with the Conus mound and its ring to the south. The town of Marietta was laid out over it in 1788; the Conus mound survives in Mound Cemetery.
notes: The squares and the graded way are gone under streets. What the LiDAR still shows: the Conus mound and its ring ditch in Mound Cemetery, and two raised blocks where the flat-topped mounds Quadranaou and Capitolium stood (the county library sits on Capitolium).
Too little wall survives for the automatic search, so this plate is placed by three hand-picked points: the Conus mound and the two platform mounds.
Charles Whittlesey surveyed it in 1837, with the town's streets drawn in; the same streets are still there.

plate.source: Squier & Davis 1848, Plate XXVI (surveyed by Charles Whittlesey, 1837). Scan: Internet Archive ancientmonuments00squi leaf n169.
plate.label: Plate XXVI

sites.name: Newark Works
sites.summary: The largest set of geometric earthworks known: an octagon joined to a circle, a 1200 ft great circle, a square and miles of parallel walls. Most of it now lies under the city of Newark. The Octagon and the Great Circle survive.
notes: Only the Octagon with its attached circle and the Great Circle still stand; the plate's square, parallel walls and small circles lie under streets and houses.
The overlay is rubber-sheeted: each surviving feature is fitted to its LiDAR walls on its own, because the plate's bearing from the Octagon to the Great Circle is about 7 degrees off.
The Great Circle walls stand over a metre above the ground beside them, the highest of any site here.

plate.source: Squier & Davis 1848, Plate XXV (surveyed by Charles Whittlesey, E. G. Squier and E. H. Davis, 1836-47). Scan: Internet Archive ancientmonuments00squi leaf n161.
plate.label: Plate XXV
